ety.text: From Middle English cotoun, from Anglo-Norman cotun, Old French coton, from (Genoese) Old Italian cotone, from Arabic قُطُن (quṭun), from Hebrew כֻּתֹּנֶת (kuttṓnĕṯ).

First use appears c. the 1560s, either from Welsh cydun, cytun (“agree, coincide”) (cyduno, cytuno), from cyd, cyt + un (“one”), literally “to be at one with”, or by metaphor with the textile, as cotton blended well with other textiles, notably wool in hat-making.

senses.d: A soft, fibrous, usually white substance consisting of fine hairs, especially the substance around the seeds of a plant of genus Gossypium.
Any similar soft, fibrous, white substance of fine hairs, of any origin.
A plant of genus Gossypium, used as a source of such fiber.
ex: K'a-shih has the most extensive cotton-growing area which amounted to 950 000 mou (6.3 million ares) in 1965.

senses.d: Any plant that encases its seed in a thin fiber that is harvested and used as a fabric or cloth.
Textiles made from the fiber harvested from a cotton plant, especially Gossypium.
An item of clothing made from such textiles.
ex: The old man wore the simplest cottons, faded from long use and countless washings.

senses.d: A small piece of cotton used as a filter when drawing up a drug into a syringe.
ex: Do not re-use needles; use fresh cottons each time.

senses.d: Thread of such fiber.
A wick of a candle.
Made of cotton.
To provide with cotton.
ex: Eyes closed, ears cottoned, the mind produces its own interior messages.

senses.d: To supply with a cotton wick.
To fill with a wad of cotton.
ex: First comes bottling, which is done both by machine and by hand. This is followed by cottoning and capping.

senses.d: To wrap with a protective layer of cotton fabric.
ex: I went round and quietly cottoned all the nine holes, and next moring I found all the cottons intact.

senses.d: To cover walls with fabric.
ex: The rooms downstairs were cottoned, the doors re-hung, and a counter put in the record office.
Robinson, W., Whitehorse: cottoning and papering 10 rooms, hall and staircase, at sergeant's mess, $206;

senses.d: To cover with cotton bolls over a layer of tar (analogous to tar and feather )
To raise a nap, providing with a soft, cottony texture.
ex: The finishing operations consisted of shearing the nap from the cloth, and frizzing, or cottoning, the surface, by pressing with hot irons.
Webs made from them had to be frizzed or cottoned.

senses.d: To develop a porous, cottony texture.
ex: Used at medium to thin consistency to avoid stringing or cottoning and to assure proper spreading characteristics.

senses.d: To give the appearance of being dotted with cotton balls.
ex: A fair piece ahead, in answering signal cottoned the sky in rhythmic puffs.

senses.d: To enshroud with a layer of whiteness.
ex: Fog cottoned the steep, wooded slopes on each side of the lake, and the air was chill and penetrating.
Fog cottoned the roads under a sky like rusted tin.

senses.d: To get on with someone or something; to have a good relationship with someone.
ex: What meanes this? doth he dote so much of this strange harlot indeed? now I perceiue how this geare cottens.
I want to tell you the Dukes, both mother and son, are cottoning to her fast enough.

senses.d: A liking.

grp.label: any plant yielding fiber like that of Gossypium

ety.text: Inherited from Old French cotoun, coton, from Italian cotone, from Arabic قُطُن (quṭun), variants of Arabic قُطْن (quṭn); see cotton for more.
Borrowed from Arabic قُطُن (quṭun); see cotton for more.

Aramaic כִיתָנָא /כִיתָאנָא (kittānā)bor. Classical Syriac ܟܶܬܳܢܳܐ (kettānā)bor. Arabic قُطْن (quṭn) Andalusian Arabic قطن (quṭun)bor. Old Spanish algodon Spanish algodón Inherited from Old Spanish algodon, from Andalusian Arabic قطن (quṭun), from Arabic قُطُن (quṭun).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic القُطُن (al-quṭun), variant of Arabic قُطْن (quṭn); see cotton for more. Doublet of cotão.

From Medieval Latin bombacium, Byzantine Greek βαμβάκιον (bambákion), from either Ancient Greek βάμβαξ (bámbax, “cotton”) or Ancient Greek βόμβυξ (bómbux, “silk-worm”), whose ultimate origin is unknown. Compare Greek βαμβάκι (vamváki), Venetan bonbaxo, Middle Persian pmbk' (pambag).

ety.text: Late Middle English, from Anglo-Norman cotage and Medieval Latin cotagium, from Old Northern French cot, cote (“cottage, hut”) + -age (“surrounding property”), from Old Norse kot, from Proto-Germanic *kutą, *kuta- (“shed”), probably of non-Indo-European origin, possibly borrowed from Proto-Finno-Ugric/Proto-Uralic *kota (“hut, tent”), probably akin to Proto-Iranian *kátah (“house; roof”). However, also compare Dutch and English hut.

senses.d: A small house.
A seasonal home of any size or stature, a recreational home or a home in a remote location.
ex: Most cottages in the area were larger and more elaborate than my home.

To stay at a seasonal home, to go cottaging.
To have homosexual sex in a public lavatory; to practice cottaging.
